subject: Chemistry
chapter: Some Basic Concepts Of Chemistry - Mole Concept

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Need for a Counting Unit: In chemistry, particles like atoms and molecules are extremely small, and even tiny amounts of substances contain vast numbers of these particles.

  • Atomic Weight: (Relative atomic mass) is defined as the weighted average mass of the atoms of an element, measured relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
  • Measured in atomic mass units (amu).
  • The average mass of atoms of an element (Calculated using the relative abundance of isotopes).
  • Molecular Weight: (Molecular mass) is the sum of the atomic weights of all the atoms in a molecule. It represents the mass of a single molecule of a substance and is typically expressed in atomic mass units (amu) or unified atomic mass units (u).
  • $\textbf{Gram atomic mass} = \text{mass of 1 gram atom} = \text{mass of 1 mole atom} = \text{mass of } N_A \text{ atoms} = \text{mass of } 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ atoms.}$
  • $\textbf{Gram molecular mass} = \text{mass of 1 gram molecule} = \text{mass of 1 mole molecule} = \text{mass of } N_A \text{ molecules} = \text{mass of } 6.022 \times 10^{23} \text{ molecules}$
  • Molar Mass: The mass of one mole of a substance is called its molar mass, which is expressed in grams per mole (g/mol).

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
$\textbf{Atomic Weight} = \frac{\text{Actual mass of one atom of the element}}{\frac{1}{12} \text{ of the mass of one atom of carbon-12}}$

$1 \ \textbf{amu} = \frac{1}{12} \ \text{of the mass of one carbon-12 atom}$

$1 \ \textbf{amu} = 1.67 \times 10^{-24} \ \text{g}$

$\textbf{Molecular Weight} = $

$\sum \left( \text{number of atoms of each element} \times \right. \\ \left. \text{atomic weight of each element} \right)$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
If an element has two isotopes, A with a mass of 10 amu and a natural abundance of 70%, and B with a mass of 12 amu and a natural abundance of 30%, what is the average atomic mass of the element?

A) 10.6 amu
B) 11.2 amu
C) 11.4 amu
D) 12.0 amu
blocks.answer:
Correct Answer: A) 10.6 amu

Solution:

Average Atomic Mass=(0.70×10amu)+(0.30×12amu)

=7.0 amu +3.6 amu

=7.0amu+3.6amu

=10.6 amu

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Atomic Weight vs. Mass Number: Confusing atomic weight (a weighted average) with mass number (total protons and neutrons).
  • Calculation Error: Using atomic weight instead of molecular weight in stoichiometric calculations.
  • While converting between grams and moles, ensure that the molar mass used in calculations is accurate and relates to the substance given in question.

blocks.title: Specific Strategy
blocks.text:
• Quick Calculation: For diatomic molecules like O₂, multiply the atomic weight by 2 for molecular weight.
  • Practice Problems: Calculate molecular weights using periodic table data for compounds like H₂O, CO₂, and NaCl.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Mole concept addresses the challenge of working with the incredibly large numbers of atoms, molecules, or ions present in measurable amounts of substances. Here are the main points that capture the introduction and core idea of the mole concept
  • Definition of a Mole: The mole (mol) was introduced as a unit for measuring the amount of substance. One mole is defined as the amount of any substance that contains as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.) as there are in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12. This number is Avogadro's number, approximately $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles.
  • It facilitates conversion between moles and the number of particles for quantitative analysis.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
$\textbf{Mole of atoms} = \frac{\text{weight (g)}}{\text{Gram atomic weight}}$

$\textbf{Mole of molecules} = \frac{\text{weight (g)}}{\text{Gram molecular weight}}$

$\textbf{Mole of atoms} = \text{atomicity} \times \text{mole of molecules}$

$\textbf{Mole of gas} = \frac{V}{22.4} \quad (V = \text{Volume of gas in litres at NTP or STP})$

$\textbf{Number of moles} = \frac{\text{Number of particles}}{N_A}
$ ($N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$)

$\textbf{Mole of atoms} = \frac{\text{Number of atoms}}{N_A}
$

$\textbf{Moles of molecules} = \frac{\text{Number of molecules}}{N_A}
$

$\textbf{Molecular weight of gas} = 2 \times \text{Vapour density}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• The percentage composition of a compound tells you the proportion by mass of each element within the compound. It’s an important concept in chemistry, especially when analyzing the makeup of compounds and determining formulas.

• Percentage composition is the mass percentage of each element in a compound relative to the total mass of the compound.

• An empirical formula represents the simplest whole-number ratio of elements in a compound, showing the relative proportions of each element without indicating the actual number of atoms in a molecule. It differs from a molecular formula, which specifies the actual number of each type of atom in a molecule.

• The molecular formula of a compound specifies the actual number of atoms of each element in a single molecule. Unlike the empirical formula, which shows only the simplest whole-number ratio, the molecular formula may show multiples of these ratios, giving the true composition of a molecule.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• For any element in a compound, the percentage composition is calculated as:

$\text{Percentage of Element} = \left( \frac{\text{Atomicity x Atomic Mass of Element}}{\text{Molar Mass of Compound}} \right) \times 100$

Calculate Empirical Formula:

  • Convert the mass or percentage of each element to moles.
  • Divide by the smallest number of moles.
  • Round to the nearest whole number.
$\text{Empirical Formula} = \frac{\text{Moles of each element}}{\text{Smallest number of moles}}$

  • Determine Molecular Formula:
  • Use the empirical formula and the compound's molar mass.
$\text{Molecular Formula} = (\text{Empirical Formula})_n$

Where $n = \frac{\text{Molar Mass}}{\text{Empirical Formula Mass}}$

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Calculate the percentage composition of oxygen in sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$​).

1. 32.69%
2. 65.31%
3. 50.00%
4. 98.00%
blocks.answer:
Solution:

Determine the Molar Mass of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$

• Hydrogen (H): 1.0 g/mol×2=2.0 g/mol.

• Sulfur (S): 32 g/mol.
    • Oxygen (O): 16.00 g/mol×4=64.00 g/mol
    • Total molar mass of $H_2SO_4$ =2+32.07+64.00=98.0 g/mol

$\text{Percentage of Element} = \left( \frac{\text{Atomicity x Atomic Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass of Compound}} \right)  \times 100$

$\text{Percentage of Element} = \left( \frac{\text{4 x 16}}{\text{98}} \right) \times 100$

≈65.31%

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question: Given the following elemental composition: C = 40%, H = 6.7%, O = 53.3%, find the empirical formula. Also find the molecular formula, if the vapour density of the molecule is 90.
blocks.answer:
Solution

  • Convert percentages to grams (assuming 100 g total): C = 40 g, H = 6.7 g, O = 53.3 g.
  • Convert grams to moles:
  • C: $\frac{40}{12.01} = 3.33 \text{ moles}$
  • H: $\frac{6.7}{1.008} = 6.65 \text{ moles}$
  • O: $\frac{53.3}{16.00} = 3.33 \text{ moles}$
  • Divide by the smallest number of moles:
  • C: $\frac{3.33}{3.33} = 1$
  • H: $\frac{6.65}{3.33} = 2$
  • O: $\frac{3.33}{3.33} = 1$
  • Empirical formula is CH₂O.
  • Empirical mass = (C+ 2H + O) = 12 +(2X1) + 16 = 30
  • Molecular mass = 2 x VD = 2 x 90 = 180
  • $n = \frac{\text{Molar Mass}}{\text{Empirical Formula Mass}}$ = 180/30 = 6
  • $\text{Molecular Formula} = (\text{Empirical Formula})_n$
$\text{Molecular Formula} = (\text{CH₂O})_6$.

$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$.

  • Confusing empirical and molecular formulas: Remember, empirical is the simplest ratio.
  • Forgetting to multiply the empirical formula by $n$ to obtain the molecular formula.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Stoichiometry is the study of the quantitative relationships between the amounts of reactants and products in a chemical reaction.
  • It Involves calculating reactants and products using a balanced equation.
  • Limiting reagent (or limiting reactant) is fundamental in chemistry, especially in stoichiometry. It refers to the substance in a chemical reaction that is entirely consumed first, thereby determining the maximum amount of product that can be formed.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Mole Ratio:
$\text{Mole Ratio} = \frac{\text{Coefficient of A}}{\text{Coefficient of B}}$
  • Limiting Reagent Identification:
Compare moles of reactants using mole ratios to find the limiting reagent.

  • Product Calculation:
$\text{Moles of Product} = \text{Moles of Limiting Reagent} \times \frac{\text{Coefficient of Product}}{\text{Coefficient of Limiting Reagent}}$
  • Mass to Moles Conversion:
$\text{Moles} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}}$

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
In the complete combustion of propane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8​$), how many moles of $\text{O}_2$ are required to completely react with 2 moles of propane?

The balanced combustion equation is:    $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$

$\text{A) } 5 \, \text{moles} \\ \text{B) } 10 \, \text{moles} \\ \text{C) } 15 \, \text{moles} \\ \text{D) } 20 \, \text{moles}$
blocks.answer:
Solution:

  • Identify the Mole Ratio: According to the balanced equation, 1 mole of propane    ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$) reacts with 5 moles of oxygen ($\text{O}_2$).
  • Set Up a Proportion: Since we have 2 moles of propane, we can calculate the required moles of oxygen based on the mole ratio:
$1 \, \text{mole of } \text{C}_3\text{H}_8 : 5 \, \text{moles of } \text{O}_2$

$\text{For 2 moles of } \text{C}_3\text{H}_8, \text{ the moles of } \text{O}_2 \text{ needed would be : }  2 \times 5          = 10 \, \text{moles of } \text{O}_2$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Concentration: Amount of solute in a given quantity of solvent or solution, determining solution strength.
  • Solution Chemistry: Study of homogeneous mixtures and solute-solvent interactions.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• $\text{Molarity (M)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution(L)}}
$
• $\text{Molality (m)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{weight of solvent(kg)}}$

• $\text{Normality (N)} = \frac{\text{equivalents of solute}}{\text{volume of solution(L)}}
$
    • $\textstyle m = \frac{M \cdot 1000}{ \rho \cdot 1000 - {M \cdot M_s}}

$
    • M = Molarity (mol/L)

m = Molality (mol/kg)

ρ = Density of the solution (g/mL)

Ms​ = Molar mass of the solute (g/mol)

  • Percent Composition:
  • Weight/Weight % (w/w%): $\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}}\times 100$
  • Volume/Volume % (v/v%): $\frac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}}\times 100$
  • Weight/Volume % (w/v%): $\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}}\times 100$
  • Parts Per Million (ppm): $ppm=\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}}\times 10^6$
Useful for: Very dilute solutions.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• The concept of gram equivalents is essential for accurately calculating and understanding the reactivity and stoichiometry of chemical substances in various reactions. It provides a practical way to work with substances in scenarios where their individual reactivity varies, enabling chemists to perform more accurate and meaningful calculations.

• The gram equivalent (or gram equivalent weight) is a crucial aspect of stoichiometry in chemistry, particularly in the context of reactions involving acids, bases, and redox processes.
    • The law of chemical equivalence, also known as the law of equivalent proportions, is a principle in chemistry that states that when two substances react with each other, they do so in definite proportions by mass that are equivalent to their equivalent weights. This concept is closely associated with stoichiometry and the idea of chemical equivalents, which refer to the amount of one substance that can react with or displace a fixed amount of another substance in a chemical reaction.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• The equivalent weight can be calculated using the formula:

$\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{\text{Atomic Mass/ Molecular Mass}}{n  factor}$

  • The gm equivalent can be calculated using the formula:
$\text{Gram Equivalent} = \frac{\text{Weight in grams}}{\text{Equivalent Weight}}$

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
What is the equivalent weight of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) if its molar mass is 98 g/mol and it can donate two protons (H⁺ ions) in a reaction?

1) 24.5 g/equiv
2) 49 g/equiv
3) 98 g/equiv
4) 196 g/equiv
blocks.answer:
Solution:

To calculate the equivalent weight, you can use the formula:

$\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{\text{Atomic Mass/ Molecular Mass}}{n  factor}$

Where:

• Molar Mass of H₂SO₄ = 98 g/mol

  • n factor (number of protons donated by H₂SO₄) = 2
  • $\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{98 \, \text{g/mol}}{2} = 49 \, \text{g/equiv}$

blocks.question:
A laboratory technician prepares a solution by dissolving 196 grams of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).  how many gram equivalents of H₂SO₄ are present in the solution?

1) 2.00 equiv
2) 3.00 equiv
3) 4.00 equiv
4) 5.00 equiv
blocks.answer:
Solution:

Using the formula:

• $\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{\text{Atomic Mass/ Molecular Mass}}{n  factor}$
    • Molar Mass of H₂SO₄ = 98 g/mol
    • n factor (number of protons donated by H₂SO₄) = 2
    • $\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{98 \, \text{g/mol}}{2} = 49 \, \text{g/equiv}$
    • Given weight of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) = 196 grams.

  • $\text{Gram Equivalent} = \frac{\text{Weight in grams}}{\text{Equivalent Weight}}$
• $\text{Gram Equivalent} = \frac{\text{196 gm}}{\text{49 gm/equiv}}$= 4 equiv

blocks.text:
• Understanding the concepts of equivalent weight and gm equivalent can sometimes lead to common mistakes.
    • Equivalent Weight refers to the mass of a substance that can react with or replace one mole of hydrogen ions (H⁺) or one mole of electrons. It is calculated as:

$\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{\text{Atomic Mass/ Molecular Mass}}{n factor}$

• Gram Equivalent is the number of equivalents of a substance present in a given weight. It is calculated as:

$\text{Gram Equivalent} = \frac{\text{Weight}}{\text{Equivalent Weight}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Law of Conservation of Mass: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
  • Law of Definite Proportions: A given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by mass.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole number ratios.
  • Gay-Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes: Gases react together in volumes which bear a simple whole number ratio to one another and to the volumes of the products, if gaseous, at constant temperature and pressure.
  • Avogadro’s Hypothesis: Equal volumes of gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain an equal number of molecules.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Law of Conservation of Mass: $m_{\text{reactants}} = m_{\text{products}}$
  • Law of Definite Proportions: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \text{constant}$ for a compound $A_xB_y$.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{n_1}{n_2}$, where $m_1, m_2$ are masses of elements, and $n_1, n_2$ are small whole numbers.
  • Gay-Lussac's Law: Volume ratios are simple whole numbers at constant temperature and pressure.
  • Avogadro's Hypothesis: $V \propto n$ at constant temperature and pressure.
  • Constants: Proportional constants in chemical reactions.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Two elements, A and B, combine to form two compounds. In the first compound, 14 g of A combine with 8 g of B. In the second compound, 14 g of A combine with 16 g of B. Verify if the Law of Multiple Proportions holds true and choose the correct option for the ratio of masses of B that combine with a fixed mass of A.

$\\ (1.) \, 1:2 \\ (2.) \, 2:3 \\ (3.) \, 3:4 \\ (4.) \, 1:3$
blocks.answer: The masses of B that combine with a fixed mass of A are in the ratio 1:2, satisfying the Law of Multiple Proportions.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not considering closed systems in the Law of Conservation of Mass.
  • Confusing the Law of Definite Proportions with the Law of Multiple Proportions.
  • Forgetting the conditions of constant temperature and pressure in Gay-Lussac's Law.
  • Neglecting equal volume condition in Avogadro’s Hypothesis.
ADDITIONAL GUIDELINES

  • Use the acronym CMDGA to remember the laws: Conservation, Multiple, Definite, Gay-Lussac, Avogadro.
  • For stoichiometric calculations, always start by checking the Law of Conservation of Mass.

• $\text{Molality (m)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{weight of solvent(kg)}}$

• $\text{Normality (N)} = \frac{\text{equivalents of solute}}{\text{volume of solution(L)}}
$
    • $\textstyle m = \frac{M \cdot 1000}{ \rho \cdot 1000 - {M \cdot M_s}}

$
    • M = Molarity (mol/L)

m = Molality (mol/kg)

ρ = Density of the solution (g/mL)

Ms​ = Molar mass of the solute (g/mol)

  • Percent Composition:
  • Weight/Weight % (w/w%): $\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}}\times 100$
  • Volume/Volume % (v/v%): $\frac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}}\times 100$
  • Weight/Volume % (w/v%): $\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}}\times 100$
  • Parts Per Million (ppm): $ppm=\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}}\times 10^6$
Useful for: Very dilute solutions.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• The equivalent weight can be calculated using the formula:

$\text{Equivalent Weight} = \frac{\text{Atomic Mass/ Molecular Mass}}{n  factor}$

  • The gm equivalent can be calculated using the formula:
$\text{Gram Equivalent} = \frac{\text{Weight in grams}}{\text{Equivalent Weight}}$

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Law of Conservation of Mass: $m_{\text{reactants}} = m_{\text{products}}$
  • Law of Definite Proportions: $\frac{m_A}{m_B} = \text{constant}$ for a compound $A_xB_y$.
  • Law of Multiple Proportions: $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{n_1}{n_2}$, where $m_1, m_2$ are masses of elements, and $n_1, n_2$ are small whole numbers.
  • Gay-Lussac's Law: Volume ratios are simple whole numbers at constant temperature and pressure.
  • Avogadro's Hypothesis: $V \propto n$ at constant temperature and pressure.
  • Constants: Proportional constants in chemical reactions.
